title: Maize Leaf Blight
summary: A fungal disease (Turcicum / Northern leaf blight) that makes long grey-green or tan lesions on maize leaves and spreads in warm, humid weather.
symptoms: Long, elliptical grey-green or tan lesions 3–15 cm long on the leaves
Lesions usually start on the lower leaves and move up the plant
Leaves may dry out and die early when many lesions join together
In humid weather a dark, dusty layer of spores may appear on the lesions
causes: Fungus (Exserohilum turcicum) surviving on old maize residue
Warm temperatures (18–27 °C) with long periods of leaf wetness
Dense planting and poor air circulation
Planting maize in the same field year after year
prevention: Rotate maize with beans or other non-grass crops
Remove or bury old maize residue after harvest
Use recommended spacing so leaves dry quickly
Choose tolerant varieties where available
actions: Remove and destroy heavily affected lower leaves to reduce spread
Improve air circulation by controlling weeds and avoiding over-crowding
Avoid overhead watering late in the day
Ask your local extension officer about locally approved fungicide options if the disease appears before tasselling
Monitor other plants every few days for 2 weeks

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Long, elliptical grey-green or tan lesions on leaves, starting on lower leaves. Lesions can join and dry the whole leaf.

sections.heading: Why it happens
sections.body: A fungal disease favoured by warm, humid conditions, dense planting and maize residue left in the field.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Remove heavily affected leaves, improve air circulation, rotate crops, and ask your extension officer about locally approved treatments.

title: Maize Leaf Rust
summary: Small orange-brown powdery pustules scattered over both leaf surfaces; usually minor but can reduce yield when severe.
symptoms: Small round to oval orange-brown pustules on both sides of the leaf
Pustules rub off as an orange powder on your fingers
Pustules darken to black late in the season
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and dry
causes: Rust fungus (Puccinia species) spread by wind-borne spores
Cool to mild temperatures with high humidity and dew
Late-planted or stressed maize is more affected
prevention: Plant early in the season so the crop matures before rust builds up
Use tolerant varieties where available
Keep plants well nourished; stressed plants suffer more
actions: Usually no treatment is needed if only a few pustules appear after tasselling
If rust is heavy on young plants, ask your extension officer about options
Remove badly affected leaves and keep the field weed-free
Note the date; plant earlier next season

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Small orange-brown pustules on both leaf surfaces that rub off as powder.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Mild rust after tasselling rarely needs treatment. Plant earlier and keep plants healthy. Seek advice if young plants are heavily affected.

title: Maize Gray Leaf Spot
summary: Narrow, rectangular grey-tan spots that run between the leaf veins; builds up late in the season in humid weather and where maize follows maize.
symptoms: Small tan spots that lengthen into narrow rectangles bounded by the leaf veins
Spots turn grey and can join into large dead strips
Starts on lower leaves 2–3 weeks after silking and moves up
Distinct from leaf blight: blight lesions are wider, oval and cross the veins
causes: Fungus (Cercospora zeae-maydis) surviving on maize residue on the soil surface
Long periods of high humidity and leaf wetness (fog, dew, light rain)
Maize planted into last season's maize stubble without rotation
prevention: Rotate maize with beans or other non-grass crops for at least one season
Bury or remove maize residue after harvest
Use tolerant varieties where available and avoid very dense planting
actions: Confirm by looking for rectangular spots bounded by the veins
Remove heavily affected lower leaves if the crop is still young
Plan a rotation to beans in this field next season
Ask your extension officer about approved fungicide options if spots appear before silking
Monitor weekly; damage after grain fill is usually minor

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Narrow rectangular grey-tan spots that stay between the leaf veins, starting on lower leaves late in the season.

sections.heading: Why it happens
sections.body: A fungus that survives on maize residue and spreads in long humid periods; worst when maize follows maize.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Remove affected lower leaves on young crops, rotate to beans next season, and seek advice if it appears before silking.

title: Maize Nutrient Stress (Yellowing)
summary: Yellow or purple leaves without spots usually mean the plant is short of nutrients or water rather than diseased.
symptoms: Yellowing that starts at the tip of older, lower leaves and runs down the midrib in a V shape (nitrogen)
Purple or reddish leaves on young plants (phosphorus, often in cold or wet soil)
Yellow edges on older leaves while the middle stays green (potassium)
Pale stripes between the veins of young leaves (zinc or iron)
No spots, lesions or holes
causes: Low soil fertility or continuous cropping without compost or fertiliser
Waterlogging or drought stopping the roots from taking up nutrients
Very acidic or very alkaline soil
prevention: Add compost or manure before planting every season
Rotate or intercrop with legumes (beans) to add nitrogen
Improve drainage on wet fields and mulch on dry fields
actions: Check soil moisture first — water stress causes similar yellowing
Top-dress with compost, manure tea or a nitrogen fertiliser at the recommended rate
Apply near the plant row and water in
If leaves are purple on young plants, wait for warmer weather and improve drainage
Ask your extension officer about a soil test if the problem repeats

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Yellowing of older leaves from the tip in a V shape usually means nitrogen shortage. Purple young leaves point to phosphorus. There are no spots or lesions.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Check water first, then top-dress with compost or nitrogen. Plant beans in rotation to build soil fertility.

title: Rice Blast
summary: The most damaging rice disease: diamond-shaped spots with grey centres on leaves, and rotting at the neck of the panicle.
symptoms: Diamond- or spindle-shaped spots with grey-white centres and brown edges on leaves
Spots join and kill large parts of the leaf
Brown-black rot at the neck of the panicle causing empty, white heads
Seedlings in the nursery may die
causes: Fungus (Magnaporthe oryzae) spread by wind and water splash
Long periods of leaf wetness, cool nights and cloudy days
Too much nitrogen fertiliser
Drought stress in rain-fed fields
prevention: Use resistant varieties recommended locally
Do not apply excessive nitrogen; split the dose
Keep the field flooded evenly during tillering
Burn or bury infected straw after harvest
actions: Stop nitrogen top-dressing when blast appears
Keep water in the field; drought makes blast worse
Remove severely infected seedlings in the nursery
Ask your extension officer about approved fungicide treatment if the disease reaches the neck stage

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Diamond-shaped leaf spots with grey centres and brown borders; neck rot causing empty panicles.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Stop extra nitrogen, keep the field flooded, remove infected seedlings and seek advice before the panicle stage.

title: Rice Bacterial Leaf Blight
summary: Water-soaked stripes along the leaf edges that turn yellow then white, spreading fast after heavy rain and wind.
symptoms: Water-soaked, yellow to white stripes starting at the leaf tips and edges
Stripes have wavy margins and spread downward
Whole leaves dry out; seedlings wilt (kresek)
Milky bacterial ooze on cut leaves in the morning
causes: Bacteria (Xanthomonas oryzae) entering through wounds and leaf pores
Heavy rain, strong wind and flooding that spread the bacteria
High nitrogen and dense planting
prevention: Use resistant varieties and clean seed
Avoid excess nitrogen
Do not clip seedling tips at transplanting
Keep bunds and channels clean of infected straw
actions: Drain the field for a few days to slow the spread
Stop nitrogen fertiliser until the crop recovers
Remove and burn heavily infected plants
Do not move through wet, infected fields into healthy ones

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Yellow-white stripes from the leaf tip and edges with wavy margins; seedlings can wilt.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Drain briefly, stop nitrogen, remove heavily infected plants and avoid spreading through wet fields.

title: Rice Brown Spot
summary: Small oval brown spots with grey centres, usually a sign that the soil is poor or the crop is short of water or potassium.
symptoms: Small oval or circular brown spots, about the size of a sesame seed, scattered over the leaf
Older spots have a grey or whitish centre with a dark brown edge
Spots appear on lower leaves first and can cover the whole leaf when severe
Brown spots may also appear on the grain husks, giving discoloured rice
causes: Fungus (Bipolaris oryzae) carried on seed and crop residue
Poor or unbalanced soil — especially low potassium or silicon
Water stress in rain-fed fields, or uneven flooding
Repeated rice cropping without adding organic matter
prevention: Use clean, treated seed from a healthy crop
Add compost or manure before planting to build soil fertility
Keep water even in the field; avoid drying out during grain filling
Remove and bury infected straw and stubble after harvest
actions: Check whether the field dried out or is short of nutrients — brown spot is usually a soil and water problem, not just a disease
Apply compost or a balanced fertiliser with potassium at the recommended local rate
Keep the water level steady, especially from flowering to grain filling
Remove badly affected lower leaves and keep the bunds weed-free
Ask your extension officer about seed treatment before the next planting

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Small oval brown spots the size of a sesame seed, with grey centres, starting on the lower leaves. Grains may also be discoloured.

sections.heading: Why it happens
sections.body: A fungus that thrives when the crop is stressed — poor soil (especially low potassium), uneven water or drought. It was the disease behind the Bengal famine of 1943.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Fix the soil and water first: add compost or potassium and keep the water level steady. Use clean seed next season and bury infected straw.

title: Tomato Early Blight
summary: Brown spots with concentric rings (target spots) on older leaves, common in warm humid weather and on stressed plants.
symptoms: Brown spots with dark concentric rings like a target on older, lower leaves
Yellow halo around each spot
Leaves yellow and drop from the bottom of the plant upward
Dark sunken spots near the stem end of fruit
causes: Fungus (Alternaria solani) surviving in soil and plant debris
Warm temperatures with high humidity or dew
Soil splashing onto lower leaves during watering or rain
Plants stressed by poor nutrition or heavy fruit load
prevention: Mulch the soil to stop splash
Stake plants and remove the lowest leaves
Water at the base in the morning, never on the leaves
Rotate with maize or beans; do not follow tomato, chili or potato
actions: Remove and destroy spotted lower leaves
Improve airflow by pruning and spacing
Feed the plant with compost to reduce stress
Ask your extension officer about approved copper or other fungicide options if spread continues

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Brown target-like spots with rings on older leaves, yellow halo, leaves dropping from the bottom.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Remove affected leaves, mulch, water at the base, stake and prune, and seek advice on approved treatments.

title: Tomato Late Blight
summary: Fast-spreading water-soaked patches that turn brown-black with white mould underneath; can destroy a crop in days during cool wet weather.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked patches on leaves that turn brown-black
White fuzzy mould on the underside of leaves in the morning
Brown, greasy patches on stems and fruit
Whole plant collapses quickly in wet weather
causes: Water mould (Phytophthora infestans) spread by wind and rain
Cool nights (10–20 °C) with high humidity and long leaf wetness
Nearby infected tomato or potato plants
prevention: Grow tomatoes in the drier months or under rain shelter
Wide spacing, staking and pruning for airflow
Never water the leaves
Remove volunteer tomato and potato plants
actions: Act fast: remove and bury or burn infected plants immediately
Do not compost infected material
Harvest healthy fruit early
Ask your extension officer urgently about approved protective treatments for the remaining plants

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Large dark water-soaked patches with white mould underneath; the plant collapses fast in cool wet weather.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Remove infected plants immediately, harvest healthy fruit early and seek urgent advice on protecting the rest.

title: Chili Anthracnose (Fruit Rot)
summary: Sunken, dark circular spots on ripening chili fruit, often with orange or pink spore masses, common in the wet season.
symptoms: Sunken, circular dark spots on fruit that enlarge quickly
Concentric rings of orange, pink or black spores inside the spot
Fruit shrivels and drops
Occasional dark spots on leaves and stems
causes: Fungus (Colletotrichum species) carried on seed and in plant debris
Rain splash and high humidity during fruiting
Overripe fruit left on the plant
prevention: Use clean seed from healthy fruit
Plant on raised beds with mulch
Harvest fruit as soon as it ripens
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (not tomato, potato, eggplant)
actions: Pick and destroy infected fruit; do not leave it on the ground
Harvest ripe fruit promptly
Improve drainage and airflow
Ask your extension officer about approved fungicide options in a wet season

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Sunken dark circular spots on ripening fruit with orange or pink rings of spores.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Remove infected fruit, harvest promptly, keep beds well drained and seek advice on approved treatments.

title: Bean Rust
summary: Small reddish-brown pustules on bean leaves that release rusty powder; severe cases drop leaves and cut yield.
symptoms: Small raised reddish-brown pustules on the underside of leaves
Rusty powder rubs off on fingers
Yellow halo around pustules; leaves yellow and fall
causes: Rust fungus (Uromyces appendiculatus) spread by wind
Warm humid weather with dew
Dense planting
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Space plants well and avoid overhead watering
Remove crop residue after harvest
actions: Remove heavily infected leaves early
Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet
Seek advice on approved fungicide if rust appears before flowering

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Reddish-brown pustules on the underside of leaves that release rusty powder.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Remove infected leaves early, keep leaves dry and seek advice if rust appears before flowering.

title: Healthy Crop Care
summary: What a healthy leaf looks like and how to keep it that way between scans.
symptoms: Uniform green colour without spots, stripes or holes
Leaves firm and turgid, not wilted
Steady new growth from the top of the plant
prevention: Water consistently and early in the morning
Mulch to keep moisture even and stop soil splash
Feed with compost every few weeks
Walk the field twice a week and look under leaves
actions: Keep monitoring; scan again in 7 days or if anything changes
Maintain your current watering and feeding schedule
Remove weeds that compete for water and hide pests

sections.heading: Signs of health
sections.body: Uniform green leaves without spots, holes or wilting, and steady new growth.

sections.heading: Keep it that way
sections.body: Water in the morning, mulch, feed with compost and inspect the field twice a week.

title: Papaya Leaf Curl, Mosaic and Ring Spot
summary: Virus diseases of papaya that curl, mottle or ring-mark the leaves. They are spread by insects, not by rain, so the cure is controlling the insect and removing sick plants early.
symptoms: Young leaves curl downward and inward, and feel thick or leathery
Yellow and green mottled patches (mosaic) across the leaf blade
Pale rings or circles on leaves, and sometimes greasy streaks on the stem
New leaves come out small and misshapen; the plant stops growing well
Fruit may show faint rings and taste poor
causes: Papaya leaf curl virus, papaya mosaic virus or papaya ring spot virus
Spread by whitefly and by aphids feeding on the plant
Spread by cutting tools used on a sick plant and then a healthy one
Planting new papaya right next to old infected trees
prevention: Plant seedlings away from old or sick papaya trees
Control whitefly and aphids early, before the plant is large
Pull out and burn badly infected plants instead of leaving them standing
Keep the area around the trees free of weeds that host whitefly
Wash hands and tools after touching a sick plant
actions: Check the underside of young leaves for whitefly and aphids
Remove and burn plants whose leaves are badly curled or mottled
Do not take cuttings or seed from an affected plant
Watch nearby healthy trees every week for the first signs

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: Leaves curl down and thicken, or show yellow-green mottling, or pale rings. New growth is small and twisted and the plant slows down.

sections.heading: Why it happens
sections.body: These are viruses carried by whitefly and aphids, and by tools. Once a plant has a virus it cannot be cured, so the work is protecting the healthy trees.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Look under the young leaves for insects and control them. Take out badly affected plants and burn them. Do not save seed or cuttings from sick trees.

sections.heading: When to ask for help
sections.body: If several trees show signs in one season, ask an agricultural extension officer before replanting papaya in the same spot.

title: Papaya Mealybug and Mite Damage
summary: Small insects and mites that feed on papaya leaves. Unlike a virus you can usually see the pest itself, and simple physical control often works if you start early.
symptoms: White cottony clusters on leaf undersides, leaf joints and young fruit
Sticky honeydew on leaves, followed by a black sooty mould
Fine pale speckling or bronzing of the leaf, with a dusty look underneath
Leaves dry at the edges and fall early
Ants moving up and down the stem
causes: Papaya mealybug feeding on sap and excreting honeydew
Red or yellow spider mites, which build up in hot dry weather
Ants protecting mealybugs from their natural enemies
Dusty, drought-stressed plants, which mites prefer
prevention: Check young leaves and leaf joints every week
Keep the plant well watered so it is not drought-stressed
Do not let ants nest at the base of the tree
Encourage ladybirds and other natural enemies by not spraying broadly
actions: Wash off mealybugs and mites with a strong jet of water on the leaf underside
Wipe heavy mealybug clusters off with a cloth and soapy water
Cut off and burn the worst affected leaves
Control ants at the base of the stem so natural enemies can work
Repeat the washing every few days until the pest is gone

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body: White cottony clusters, sticky leaves and black sooty mould mean mealybug. Fine speckling or bronzing with dust underneath means mites.

sections.heading: Why it happens
sections.body: Both feed on the sap. Ants protect mealybugs from the insects that would eat them, and mites build up fastest on dry, dusty, stressed plants.

sections.heading: What to do
sections.body: Wash the leaf undersides with a strong jet of water, wipe heavy clusters with soapy water, cut off the worst leaves and burn them, and stop the ants.

sections.heading: When to ask for help
sections.body: If the whole tree is covered or the fruit is affected, ask an extension officer. Avoid broad sprays, which kill the natural enemies too.
